THE PURPOSE OF THIS ARTICLE is to describe the operation of a specific creative psychodynamic process, termed janusian process, in psychoanalytic treatment. Although there has been a great deal of psychoanalytic interest in creativity and designations such as "creative analyst" or "creative therapist" are decidedly honorific, few attempts have been made to describe effective treatment as a creative process. Beres (1964), drawing on Kris's (1952) concept of creativity as regression in the service of the ego, attempted to draw analogies between communication in the literary creative process and in psychoanalytic treatment. Weigert (1964) proposed that the goal of psychotherapy was creative reconstruction, which she defined as "the integration of traditional ideals and freely chosen commitments and responsibilities on the level of maturity" (p. 13). Three phases of psychoanalysis were considered by Hulbeck (1963) to be creative: 1) the encounter which arouses creative curiosity in both patient and therapist; 2) a dialogue phase in which a creative experience arises when the influence of the analyst on the patient and the patient on the analyst is reduced to a minimum; 3) an articulation phase involving the definition or redefinition of the patient's and doctor's standpoints. Literature on art, music, and poetry therapy often focus on a patient's improved artistic creativity as a result of these specialized approaches, but this particular type of improvement has not been conceptually attributed to an intrinsically creative structure of psychoanalytic therapy.

Recently, the seminal articles of Ehrenberg (1990) and Feiner (1990) on play in the psychoanalytic treatment relationship, while not focused directly on creativity, have helped to suggest some linkage. I AM HONORED TO PARTICIPATE in a symposium sponsored by this Institute, which has a proud tradition of independent thought, and a longstanding commitment to the study of processes taking place between patient and analyst. I have shared some of that same commitment myself since first reading Harry Stack Sullivan during graduate school. In this spirit, I shall focus today on the role of immediate experiences between patient and analyst in resolving unconscious transferences.

I shall present clinical vignettes which show that analytic patients may become conscious of a previously unconscious transference, and may make progress toward resolving this transference, without interpretation. The vignettes are not intended to minimize the importance of interpretation; I believe that precise interpretations are a crucial aspect of analytic work. Instead, the vignettes cast light on another crucial feature of analytic work. They show that actual experiences in the relationship between patient and analyst, even without interpretation, may correct pathogenic transference expectancies, and enable the patient to begin to resolve an unconscious transference. They also show how patients themselves work unconsciously to solve their psychological problems. Moreover, the vignettes give us some indication of the lawfulness of the relation between experiencing and gaining insight.

Ms. Y.

My first vignette is from the case of Ms. Y., a divorced professional woman who had had three previous analyses of 6 years, 9 years, and 3 years respectively. In addition, her behavior had been carefully observed and regularly interpreted from the cradle onward by her hovering father, a successful businessman, who kept a daily diary of his only child for several years.

CONCEIVABLY, THE HISTORY OF PSYCHOANALYSIS could now be recast and rewritten from the standpoint of the dialectical tension between the competing interests of the various interpretive metapsychologies and direct psychoanalytic inquiry. That new version of the history of psychoanalysis would move back and forth between the development of this field of human knowledge, seeking to coordinate the two, and the lives of individual psychoanalysts caught up in its dialectic of metapsychology and psychology, searching for their own true positions. SINCE FREUD'S CURIOSITY ABOUT WOMEN was guided by his male point of view, his attempts to shed light on the "dark continent" were colored by presumptions that consequently structured his theory. Despite his explicit wonder, Freud believed he knew what it was that women wanted and, because of their biology, could never have. In his paper, Femininity, Freud (1933/1974) wrote, "The feminine situation is only established … if the wish for a penis is replaced by one for a baby" (p. 87). For Freud, "What does a woman want?" was posed rhetorically.

In this same paper addressed to his colleagues Freud also wrote, "If you want to know more about femininity, enquire from your own experiences of life" (p. 93). Therefore, from a female analyst's perspective, I will explore the idea that what a woman wants has more to do with processing desire than with substituting acquisitions. As analyst, diagnostic understanding and interpretive selections are derived by filtering clinical data through the exquisitely sensitive instrument of the professional gendered self. Therefore, in the context of her work, "What does a woman want?" interests the female analyst because it asks her to maintain self-awareness while guiding the treatment process. I propose that the female analyst's attention to her desire in the countertransference engages a sensual element of interpersonal process that informs and enlivens the work.

Regardless of theoretical approach, the analyst and patient share a transactional field that is comprised of each participant's fantasies, wishes, and expressive style. One's identity as female or male involves the presentation and communication of underlying psychic-relational patterns influenced by cultural role expectations (Person, 1985). Dianne Farber  

THIS QUESTION HAS A BURNING immediacy for society at a time when traditional gender roles have increasingly come into question. What do women want? Recently, in a different context, I wrote that most women want "time enough to nurture their children adequately without being punished later by an unforgiving job market" (Farber, 1990). This journal has challenged me to respond further by addressing the answer given in a fifteenth century tale of King Arthur (Zimmer, 1956). If nothing else, this ancient story illustrates how long men have striven to answer this question.

The story, in poetry form, is called "The Weddynge of Sir Gawen and Dame Ragnell" (the text alternates between modern spelling and fifteenth century English. Generally I shall use the modern spellings). I will examine this tale and others to place this old question—and answer—in a modern context.

The Weddynge of Sir Gawen and Dame Ragnell

The poem describes how the unarmed King Arthur is accosted in the forest one day by a well-armed knight who believes he was deeply wronged when Arthur stole his lands and gave them to his nephew, Sir Gawain. The knight threatens to kill the king. King Arthur reminds the angry knight that he, Arthur, is unarmed; to kill an unarmed man is unsporting. Relenting, the knight tells Arthur to come to the same spot in one year and tell him the answer to the question, "What is it that a woman most desires in all the world?" If he answers wrongly, he forfeits his life.

King Arthur, perplexed, consults Sir Gawain, and they spend a year questioning both men and women for the answer. The multitude of answers fills two books, but still the king is uneasy and seeks a better answer. He meets in the forest "the most ugly hag mankind had ever seen, " with "face red, nose snotted withal, " and "hanging heavy paps." But she rides her horse gaily and richly saddled.

The hag rides up to the king and tells him immediately that none of his answers is correct.

An Announcement

Contemporary Psychoanalysis intends to publish essays from areas other than psychoanalysis. We believe that insights from different sources can illuminate psychoanalytic knowledge. It is not our intention to apply psychoanalysis to other disciplines. We believe that the arts, sciences, and the humanities have something to add to our work of understanding people and facilitating their growth.

A paper discussing the dynamics and experience of alienation, as illuminated in Dostoevsky's "Notes from the Underground" or Camus's "The Stranger, " would be appropriate, since an appreciation of these novels could be used to shed light on psychoanalytic theory and practice, as would an understanding of facing death in Mann's "Death in Venice" and Tolstoy's "The Death of Ivan Illytch." Applications of the data of cognitive psychology to psychoanalysis could be useful as well; a psychoanalytic interpretation of these would not. An anthropological perspective on interpersonal psychoanalytic theories of sexuality would be germane; psychoanalytic reflections on the politics of conservatism or nationalism would not.

We hope these examples illustrate our desire to provide opportunities for expression of the wide-ranging thoughtful curiosity that always has been significant in the development of psychoanalytic theory. We want to enrich our endeavors by drawing on ideas from the broad spectrum of intellectual interests.

Contributions are welcome.

Donnel B. Stern, Ph.D.

HOW CAN A MAN KNOW WHAT A woman's life is? A woman's life is quite different from a man's. God has ordered it so. A man is the same from the time of his circumcision to the time of his withering. He is the same before he has sought out a woman for the first time, and afterwards. But the day when a woman enjoys her first love cuts her in two. She becomes another woman on that day. The man is the same after his first love as he was before. The woman is from the day of her first love another. That continues so all through life. The man spends a night by a woman and goes away. His life and body are always the same. The woman conceives. As a mother she is another person than the woman without child. She carries the fruit of the night for nine months in her body. Something grows. Something grows into her life that never again departs from it. She is a mother. She is and remains a mother even though her child die, though all her children die. For at one time she carried the child under her heart. And it does not go out of her heart ever again. Not even when it is dead. All this the man does not know, he knows nothing. He does not know the difference before love and after love, before motherhood and after motherhood. He can know nothing. Only a woman can know that and speak of that. That is why we won't be told what to do by our husbands. A woman can only do one thing. She can respect herself. She can keep herself decent. She must always be as her nature is. She must always be maiden and always be mother. Before every love she is a maiden, after every love she is a mother. In this you can see whether she is a good woman or not.

—AN ABYSSINIAN WOMAN1

THE PLURALISTIC PERSPECTIVE ON INTERPRETATIVE metapsychology has been gaining increasing recognition in psychoanalysis. There is considerable agreement on the extraordinary variousness of the myth and metaphor by which psychoanalysts articulate their

procedures. Some psychoanalysts are also expanding the clinical field of inquiry so as to include the metapsychologies by which patients shape their therapeutic coparticipation, as well. Especially in this decade, when pluralism, democracy, and self-determination of peoples have so rapidly exploded without precedent onto the world scene, even the most hidebound psychoanalysts from all the interpretive traditions may begin to pay attention. For the dialectical tensions that hold between the conditioned and instrumental needs of the environing culture on one side, and the self-expressive and self-fulfilling needs of the individual on the other, have already begun to affect the central discussions of psychoanalytic metapsychology. But not, however, the empirical and systematic orders of psychoanalytic psychology.

How is it possible that one and the same body of knowledge can hold within itself both a pluralistic view of its interpretives and conjectures and, side by side with that, a unified view of its empirics and systematics? Because, as Taylor's work makes clear, into the complex modern philosophy of human nature and nature are built certain limits and possibilities of both human intelligence and natural intelligibility. This, in broadest outline, gives the widely ranging overview of his richly documented book. He weaves into his argument the following themes he considers fundamental to the modern mind: the inwardness of personal experience, the affirmation of ordinary life, and the place of nature in human nature. And he also considers the conflicts of modernity: in sum, what it is to be a human agent dealing with "the sense of inwardness, freedom, individuality, and being embedded in nature." Most interesting, in my view, is his attempt to show that the values of disengaged reason, best illustrated in the advanced technologies of scientific instrumentalism, and the values of expressive individualism, best illustrated in the personal experiences of self-awareness and self-fulfillment, may hang together in one and the same philosophical outlook, such that neither disappears into the overemphasis of the other. A quest for balance between freedom and order, and between innovative experiment and established truth, this work overlooks very little that is of current interest to the psychoanalytic psychologists of the self across the board, from those interested in the self as object to those interested in its psychic center.

To the Editor:

THIS LETTER IS A RESPONSE TO "Vygotsky and Piaget," by A. Tenzer (26:: 46–51). In that paper Tenzer highlighted the points of similarity between the theories of Jean Piaget and Lev Vygotsky and concluded that, overall, points of contention "seem … to be more a matter of emphasis than of a radical difference in viewpoint" (p. 50). Tenzer is not alone in this opinion (Biddell, 1988); (Rogoff, 1988), which is certainly not devoid of merit. However, in my view, a presentation of similarities alone skews the question, ignoring as it does, central paradigmatic and substantive differences. In order to allow a more fine-grained exploration of the points of comparison, I believe it would be useful to elaborate the underlying assumptions and relevant issues of the theories.

My argument revolves around a comparison of two main points: (1) paradigmatic assumptions; (2) the relationship between the individual and society in cognitive development. Related issues will be touched upon along the way.

All theories presuppose general models upon which formulations are based (Reese & Overton, 1970). These models, which have been called, variously, "paradigms" or "world views" (Kuhn, 1962) and "world hypotheses" (Pepper, 1942) embody disparate constructions of the "the way the world is," and consequently are irreconcilable.

Readers are invited to send in brief commentaries or critical evaluations of issues raised in this Journal or in the psychoanalytic field in general. These communications should be no more than eight pages, and should be addressed to the Editor.

THERE ARE MANY REASONS FOR a father's permanent absence from home. Divorce, an accidental death, death following an illness, or incarceration, for example, entail very different circumstances for the spouse, the family, and of course, the child. These circumstances will inevitably effect a developing child in very different ways. These differences notwithstanding, paternal absence in and of itself has a major developmental impact on a child.

Fatherlessness does not necessarily produce psychopathology and is not a cause for psychotherapeutic intervention. Nevertheless, the effects of a parent's absence on the process of a child's psychotherapy are significant, regardless of the disorder for which psychotherapy has been undertaken. The approach presented in this essay differentiates the problem of paternal absence from the problem of paternal loss and absence on the process of psychotherapy. To this end, the psychotherapies of several children who each lost contact with his father at a very young age will be presented. In this way, absence can be examined without the compounding problems entailed by loss. To further minimize the complexity of the problem, only the treatments of boys have been selected. From these treatments, the technical adaptations particular to the treatment of the fatherless boy will be articulated. Many of these principles will also apply to circumstances of experienced loss and absence, although in such circumstances the issue of loss may at times overshadow the issue of absence.

THE FOLLOWING PANEL WAS part of the William Alanson White Psychoanalytic Society Spring Weekend Conference held from March 30 to April 1, 1990.

Ideally becoming an analyst is always a work in progress. Growth and change continue long after graduation from an Institute. The subject of this panel highlights the discoveries, discrepancies and detours that are encountered along the way.

Although many of us hope for certainties when we begin our psychoanalytic training, sooner or later we are disabused of our illusion. We may set up analytic heros and villains only to learn, as we grow in experience, that these splits were founded on inadequate knowledge. We learn that consistency and consensus rarely exist even under one theoretical umbrella. Inevitably we integrate our work with patients and our personal and theoretical assumptions to form new patterns of understanding.

The process of separation-individuation sometimes proceeds quite out of awareness. Drs. Bromberg, Epstein and White each trace aspects of their professional development with candor and self-awareness. In their contributions that confluence of what was taught, learned and integrated results in three unique statements about the evolutionary process of becoming a psychoanalyst. THE PATIENT WAS 22 WHEN she began treatment and seven years later (with a year's interruption when she was in graduate school), we hit a stalemate or impasse which seriously undermined my understanding of what I thought we had accomplished. During this period, which lasted for six to 10 months, I could not see my way out of, or into, the knot that this woman and I seemed tied in. At times, I seriously thought I had completely misjudged what this woman was all about, or, if analysis could help her. Eventually, my despair matched the patient's. Ordinarily under these circumstances I talk to a colleague, but as I will describe, I was not truly aware of what was happening.

Before I present the clinical material, I think it is important to state why I have chosen this particular difficult time in a longterm treatment situation where there had been many periods of no apparent movement except in varying kinds of regressive behavior and feeling states. Yet I did not conceptualize those times as a stalemate.

In those earlier years, the level of her anxiety, the nightmarish qualities of her dreams, the profound conflicts she experienced in so much of her living seemed reason enough for improvement to be slow and arduous. And then, of course, there was always so much more to understand, an idea that was always comforting to me. Moreover, we had a good working relationship which would withstand the vicissitudes of her demands, her periods of rage at the slow progress she felt she was making, and her despair and anguish over what she felt was her lost life. Thus, no matter how convinced she would become at my failure to help her, she always managed to see me as an ally, however inept. For my part, I always felt that we could talk to each other no matter how tumultuous her life became or intense and negative the interaction between us. Thus, I never considered long periods of stasis as impasses, but simply that these were the problems inherent in working with this young woman.

AFTER MANY FALSE STARTS I began to wonder why I found it so difficult to set down my thoughts about this story. I gradually realized that unlike many legends that have clear "psycho-symbolic" relevance, this one did not resonate for me. If anything, it jarred. It would seem obvious to view the tale as an answer to that troublesome question, "What do women want?" However, I find it too problematic to interpret it in that light. After all, the major focus and cast of characters are questing men. Moreover, what woman could say that there is any one thing she most desires in the world, any one motivation for her complex and sometimes contradictory urges? How well could one woman's answer possibly speak for all women, much less "Woman?"

The problem became clearer as I asked myself whose voice was represented, who was the poet/storyteller and what did the story tell us about her or him? Even more fundamentally, was the "author" writing from a feminine or a masculine orientation? (I think this is a valid question, while of course the actual gender of the raconteur/narrator is unknowable, and perhaps immaterial). To what extent was this tale the product of the female psyche, and to what extent of the male psyche?

In response to these musings, my answer was that the tale seemed to me to be a reflection of a masculine sensibility more than a feminine one. One could even say that from one perspective, it is the story of the male's sincere attempt to try to understand what moves women to be as they are and to behave as they do.

The sociolinguist Deborah Tannen (1990) makes the case that women communicate in order to establish connectedness or relatedness, while men communicate primarily to establish their position in a power/status hierarchy. (Though stereotypic and certainly rather simplistic, her point is backed up with ample empirical observations and data of females and males from childhood through adulthood.)

Peter Schneider  

THIS PAPER WILL DESCRIBE SOME of the implicit aims and functions of therapeutic questioning. It should shed some light on the quality and aims of the therapeutic encounter. My discussion will be confined to the linguistic form of questioning with the understanding that this leaves out much paralinguistic, non-verbal questioning.

What distinguishes questions in the therapy situation from questions in everyday discourse is their quality as interventions, i.e., as strategic moves in the development of the relationship between therapist and patient. The therapist pursues a strategy to realize a number of immediate and long-term goals. These goals (e.g., the fostering of trust between therapist and patient, the gaining of particular insights by the patient, the inculcation of a particular attitude of the patient toward him/herself, etc.) are often implicit or ambiguous in practice. An analysis of therapeutic questioning can reveal them explicitly.

As strategy, whether or not consciously intended by the therapist, questions in the therapy situation are by nature semantically opaque. That is, it is always reasonable to look for more than one level of meaning. By contrast, in everyday discourse it is not the usual assumption that there is more than one level of meaning or purpose in a question, although there may be, in fact. Moreover, the obverse of these propositions also holds. That is, although it is reasonable to assume that any given therapeutic question is functioning as an intervention, one must also remain open to the possibility that any given question's purposes are perfectly explicit and, relatively, non-strategic.

Mourning and Melancholia

AS FREUD DESCRIBED IT, MELANCHOLIA is a condition akin to mourning with the main difference between the two being that "In mourning it is the world that has become poor and empty; in melancholia it is the ego itself" (1964, p. 51). In a condition of melancholia, an individual's response to the loss of a valued object is inextricably, and seemingly inexplicably, bound up with severe self-criticism and the loss of self-regard. As Freud acknowledges, the mental state of the mourner, isolated in dejection and preoccupied with sadness, is no less "disturbed" than that of the melancholic, but in the case of the mourner, "It is really only because we know so well how to explain it that this attitude does not seem to us pathological" (p. 49).

The purpose of this paper is to suggest the possibility that in some instances what we might be inclined to think of as melancholia or pathological grief may be a mourner's response to loss that relevant onlookers do not know so well how to explain. In other words, though Freud did not say so directly, he strongly implies that in cases of mourning or "normal" grief, there is a consonance between how the mourner understands his or her loss and how that loss is understood—and responded to—by others. It may be further argued that it is that very consonance that is a necessary (though, of course, not necessarily sufficient) precondition for the development of normal, as distinct from pathological, grief.

Had the presentations been clinical, there would always have been the possibility of constructing clever alternative formulations, or the opportunity to expand upon the ideas of the treating clinician. But how to discuss the training experiences of three fellow psychoanalysts, along with their subsequent development as clinicians, this issue of what we learned, what we do and what we teach? Was I going to be presented with three autobiographical accounts, three personal credos, or more likely, some combination of the two?

Ultimately, I resolved the matter by telling myself I would look for the hopefully not too elusive threads and follow the program chairperson's advice and keep my response brief, informal and, as much as possible, anecdotal. Additionally, circumstances allowing for this, I have decided to respond to the topic of the panel myself. Such responses as I do have to the presentations are sandwiched in amongst my own remembrances of times past and more recent.

The word carries a host of connotations from its more general English usage that tend to stay with it when applied to psychoanalysis. This migration of meaning from one frame of reference to another may carry unwarranted implications for the psychoanalytic construct, and may also lend it a false validity. No one with any power of observation has any reason to doubt the prevalence of human intransigence. Saddam Hussein offers an example on a global scale. People resist all kinds of things, a second cookie, or sitting down to prepare a paper such as this one. We resist external influences and forces, and we resist ourselves. The term readily acquires moral connotations. The French Resistance was heroic, as is all resistance of tyranny. But resisting authority, or resisting the law is likely to be frowned upon. When we resist ourselves, it is often viewed as good or as bad. Resisting the temptation of the second cookie can make us feel morally upstanding, while resisting the task of preparing the paper can make us feel a little ashamed. And our resistance of ourselves can be life long. William Jackson Bate (1975), in his biography of Samuel Johnson, comments on Johnson's lifelong struggle to develop self-discipline in his work habits and to rise early. He cites repeated diary entries setting forth new resolutions to rise early, with references to past resolutions broken, that cover the period from the age of twenty seven to the age of seventy one, a forty three year span.

All patients are resistant, some much more than others. Some clinicians even refer to resistant systems, such as whole families (Anderson & Stewart, 1983), as well as to resistant individuals. Clinicians of diverse persuasions use the term, but do they use it in the same way? Although his use of the term underwent change, Freud (1912) essentially defined it as the rising up against the work of the analysis of all those forces within the psyche that have caused the libido to regress. Note that the term referred to hypothesized internal forces, when acting in a specific context (against the work of the analysis). In Greenson's (1967) elaboration on the various sources and types of resistance, based on Freud's tripartite structure, he made it clear that virtually anything the patient does or says can serve a resistant function.

HOW ONE DEFINES RESISTANCE IS determined by one's theoretical assumptions. We know that Freud defined resistance in accordance with his structural model of the mind. If everything that is evoked by the therapeutic process can become a focus of resistance, then any psychic structure can also become a source of resistance. Accordingly, Freud listed (Freud, 1926, p. 160) five kinds of resistance—three emanating from the ego, and one from the id and superego respectively. Repression, transference resistance, and the secondary gain of illness arise from the ego. Id (instinctual) resistance, is the resistance of repetition, that which requires "working through." Super ego resistance is expressed as the sense of guilt and the need for punishment which opposes recovery and opposes the diminution of pain. Freud's use of the term resistance also included opposition to the ultimate aims of treatment, that is, resistance to recovery from neurotic suffering as well as resistance to the therapeutic process itself, such as the resistance to the acceptance of the therapist's interpretation.

No matter how resistance is defined, resistance assumes many forms which I will not attempt to elaborate.

WHEN SPEAKING ABOUT FACTORS leading to analytic cure, I think the most important work written on the subject was Freud's essay Analysis, Terminable and Interminable, which is one of his most brilliant papers, and, if one could put it that way, one of his most courageous, although Freud never lacked courage in any of his other works. It was written not long before his death, and in a way it is Freud's own last summarizing word about the effect of analytic cure. What I should like to do tonight is to first summarize briefly the main ideas of this paper and then, in the main part of this lecture, try to comment on it and possibly make some suggestions in connection with it.

First of all, what is interesting in this paper is that Freud presents in it a theory of psychoanalysis which had not really changed since the early days. His concept of neurosis is that neurosis is a conflict between instinct and the ego: either the ego is not strong enough, or the instincts are too strong, but at any rate, the ego is a dam; it is not capable of resisting the onrush of instinctual forces, and for this reason neurosis occurs. This is in line and consistent with his early theory, and he presented it also in its essence without trying to embellish or modify it. What follows from that is that analytic cure consists essentially in strengthening the ego which in infancy was too weak, enabling it to cope now with instinctual forces, in a period in which the ego would be strong enough.

BEGINNING AROUND 1950, a heated debate ignited concerning the potential usefulness of countertransference as a tool for understanding the patient. Led by Annie Reich (1951), (1960), the classical camp argued that the term countertransference should be limited to the therapist's pathological response to the patient, emanating from his own unresolved conflicts. This viewpoint was vigorously opposed by what Kernberg (1965) called the totalist perspective. Under the leadership of people like Heimann (1950) and Racker (1957), the definition of countertransference had been expanded to refer to the therapist's total response to his patient. Even powerful and enduring emotional responses to patients were considered to be potentially useful sources of understanding.

In the four intervening decades, it is clear that the classical camp has winnowed in favor of the burgeoning totalist ranks. As testimony to this inexorable shift, we may consider the recent remarks of Abend (1989), who is himself a noted classical analyst. He asserts that the controversy over the definition of countertransference in its narrow, pathological sense versus the totalistic view has been "irreversibly settled" in favor of the broader definition. Indeed, he argues that the mention of countertransference in case presentations has become a "mark of analytic professionalism, " whereas once it was a stigma.

Despite the widespread acceptance of what Sandler (1976) calls our "role-responsiveness" to patients, the issue of countertransference disclosure remains plagued by "near phobic dread" (Bollas, 1983). Articles on the topic of countertransference and psychoanalytic technique (Abend, 1989) conspicuously bypass the subject of disclosure. PSYCHOANALYSTS SEEM TO DEMONSTRATE some kind of self criticism when they move forward with revisions of theory and technique. For those of the so-called classical tradition, one might say it's sort of like draftsmen, each vying to see which one of them can draw the most nearly perfect circle or square. That is, each is trying to do the same thing better than one's predecessors, or even one's contemporaries. And as far back as 1929 Glover did remark that it was to the analyst's credit that he paid more attention to the fallibility of his measuring instruments than any other scientist of the era (Glover, 1929).

Those contemporary psychoanalysts, who became critics of this entire group by virtue of their radical conceptual shift, seem to deny that circularity and/or squareness is the true form, or that any one particular shape is, for that matter. These analysts are bent on showing that psychoanalysis is now much different than originally conceived. It is actually one, among many imperfect endeavors, which attempts to understand intercepting—sometimes indefinable—clusters of forces which represent the unending mutation of a human being's associations, connections, and individual development. We do stand on the shoulders of a giant, and we do see farther. But seeing farther can mean to see differently, that is, if we have a mind for it.

IT IS A SINGULAR OPPORTUNITY AND a privilege to be asked to discuss a previously unpublished manuscript of Erich Fromm's (Fromm, 1964/1991) ; my aim is to use the opportunity to articulate and consider some aspects of his approach to clinical psychoanalysis. Uniquely, it is one of the very few of his writings which address clinical work explicitly, even to the point of including a case illustration. Though, as the editor notes, Fromm was far better known for his contributions to social psychology, and to audiences outside of the psychoanalytic community, his clinical ideas left a powerful imprint on those who had the opportunity to know him through his supervision, much of which was done at the William Alanson White Institute over a period of more than thirty years, initially as one of the Institute's founders, in 1943, until he effectively retired from teaching in the United States in moving to Switzerland, in the mid-1970's. As far as I am aware, I was the last candidate in training at the White Institute to have had the opportunity to present extensive clinical work to him in supervision, during a seminar he conducted under the auspices of the Harry Stack Sullivan Society (the candidates' psychoanalytic organization), in 1974.

PERIODICALLY THROUGHOUT HISTORY men have posed the riddle "What do women want?" Some have even claimed to know the answer, including the writer of Genesis who condemned Eve for placing desire for knowledge above devotion to her mate and her creator. So, too, the writer of the fifteenth century poem, The Wedding of Sir Gawain and Dame Ragnell, answered decisively: "Above all things … women desire sovereignty" (1956, p. 62). To the extent that knowledge is power, these ancient answers are closely related. In a time more beleaguered by ambiguity and self doubt, Freud acknowledged the question to be beyond his powers of insight and ingenuity. Though he made a multitude of denigrating statements about female character and desire, he said with uncharacteristic modesty to Marie Bonaparte, "The great question that has never been answered and which I have not yet been able to answer despite my 30 years research into the feminine soul is what does a woman want?" (Jones, 1955, Vol. 2, p. 421).

Considering the question from my own perspective, as a middle aged, middle class, white female, and psychoanalyst/teacher/supervisor in the year 1991, I found myself in an emotional and conceptual swamp. At first eager and stimulated, then irritated, then bewildered, and at last curiously apathetic, I said to myself, "This question is impossible to answer intelligently." But, unwilling to surrender, I continued defiantly, "What makes men ask such idiotic questions?" This one is a red flag to me with its implication that women are a separate species whose murky inner workings defy analysis by men's logic and reason. And, compounding the questioner's sin, it assumes we all want alike. Who would be arrogant or imprudent enough to reply with some unitary formulation? How could this be answered without considering issues of time, place, social class, race, ethnicity and the vicissitudes of individual identity?

THE CONCEPT OF CHARACTER HOLDS a central position in psychoanalysis. However, each analytic school has different presuppositions about its origins, and how it functions within the individual. These differences in theoretical perspective have important implications for the way treatment is conducted.

Freud (1908) developed a theory of character that was organized around the libidinal strivings of the young child. He postulated that an instinct was transformed through mechanisms such as sublimation, and reaction formation. Because of the transformation, character traits were not easily identified with the instinct that gave rise to them. He hypothicated that a trio of ordinary social traits (being orderly, parsimonious, and obstinate), is the resultant transformation of anal eroticism. This perspective is consistent with Freudian treatment techniques. Whatever you see has a deeper meaning. Through the process of regression, within the transference neurosis, the analyst tries to help the patient get in touch with the underlying instinctual motivations.

In the late 1930s, Fromm, Sullivan, and a number of other analysts began to look at character development, and indeed all of human development, in a different light.

ONE OF THE PRIME DECONSTRUCTIVE functions of psychoanalysis is to question the assumptions which permeate words (Hamburg, 1989). A standard thesaurus treats standoff, impasse and stalemate as synonyms, which is what is wrong with thesauruses (or is it thesauri?). These words carry quite different implications, and I would like to suggest that Dr. Friedman is more correct than she knows when she calls her problems with this patient a "stalemate."

To put it succinctly, a standoff is what we had with Russia; i.e., no one dares move first since both participants have equal destructive power. An impasse occurs when no further progress is possible and forward movement stops, as in, say union or budget negotiations. A stalemate is something else. Stalemate is a chess term: when it is no longer possible for the losing player to move without putting his or her King in check, when there are no moves left to the player, then that player has provoked a stalemate, which is a draw. Nobody wins. In other words, provoking a stalemate is a strategy the losing player uses to avoid defeat or 'checkmate' (which, by the way, is from the Persian, shah mat, the King is dead!). I would say the patient did exactly that—forced a stalemate (stal mat), to avoid a more total capitulation.

This, of course, sounds rather bizarre. Am I suggesting that psychoanalysis is adversarial, that it is a game in which one person wins and the other loses? In a manner of speaking, I am.

When eventually the dame meets the King she can tell him, condescendingly, "If I help thee not, thou art but dead." If a commoner, and a hideous hag at that, can patronize a King so casually, women must not only desire, but actually have the power of life and death. And of course she gets her way; Arthur surrenders to her the noble and loyal Sir Gawain.

But things are not that simple. Eventually, we find out that Dame Ragnell was not born loathesome, and probably not power-mad either. She is less a fiend than a victim herself, struggling to overcome a spell cast on her by her stepmother. Her hunger for power is itself a part of the spell; she must remain hideous "until the best knight of England should wed her and yield the sovereignty of all his body and goods." So the message of the story is ambiguous. Perhaps women are power hungry villains who will stop at nothing to dominate a man. Or perhaps they are dominated by the evil machinations of others, so that their need for power is secondary to the need to survive. The question echoes through psychoanalytic theory and clinical practice even today.

The idea that women want to dominate men reflects a widely held belief that the desire for domination is a fundamental human motive.1 It is commonly assumed in popular culture, and in psychoanalytic theory as well, that those people who don't have power are seeking it and that those who have power use it to dominate others. Examples can be found in most societies, and even the animal kingdom provides a rich array of dominating behaviors. Virtually all societies include hierarchical systems like the caste system, ruling classes, pecking orders, bosses and subordinates, and authorities. In more intimate relationships the balance of power is always crucial; how much power does each individual have, and how can this be adjusted so that needs are met.

ENVY, AS A STATE OF MIND, IS OF NO particular bother when one feels able to acquire something just like or just as good as what is envied. The trouble arises when one feels that one cannot, because what rouses the envy is beyond one's hope of acquisition. At such a juncture, one must either give up the wish and one's hope for it, or create a scenario in which acquiring what one envies will be possible under a given set of circumstances. Thus of penis envy Freud wrote that the little girl may hope either later to acquire the penis (it may grow inside out from within) or symbolize it such that it can be represented by a baby or something else, The little boy may tell himself that the problem is but a matter of time and that some day he may acquire a penis the equal of his father's—and then his mother will succumb to his ardor and his charms. And in fact under favorable circumstances these scenarios may get the children through long enough for them to value that which they do possess. AS DISCUSSED IN PARTS I AND II (This Journal 26:257–290, 26:377–407), the concepts of nothingness, meaninglessness, and chaos are informed by a deficit theory, a theory of "absence" (both primary and secondary ["foreclosure", in the sense of Lacan, 1977]) in addition to a conflict theory. It is my thesis that conflicts are to be solved through resolution (dialectics) and that deficits are to be solved through self- and interactional regulation1. Further, regulation (or modulation) relates to the most basic physiological aspects of the internal milieu and of behavior with others and is ultimately based on elemental somato-psychic and psycho-somatic signals (rather than on signs or symbols). It is the "language" of primary narcissism and of symbiosis and occupies a space midway between need and desire (Lacan, 1966). The "language" of regulation is contrasted with that of symbolic function and its forerunners.

SO FEW ANALYSTS ARE WILLING ANY more to defend the blank screen metaphor of the analyst's role, at least in its stark form, sans qualifications, that to attack it has become a gratuitous act, useful only as a kind of chest-beating. And yet every time one is ready to consign the issue to oblivion, one reads some new article, or hears about someone's defense of neutrality, and the tired old argument comes to life. So perhaps the distinction between those who adhere to the orthodox clinical view and those who don't retains meaning after all.

Be that as it may, it has become much less interesting to bash the blank screen metaphor than to delineate differences within the group of analysts who already accept some kind of modification of the most conservative view. Work in this area has only just begun. One of the few comparisons of this sort is by Greenberg and Mitchell (1983), who describe three solutions to the problem of how to represent interpersonal relations in psychoanalytic theory: One can, like Freud himself, along with Hartmann, Mahler, Jacobson, and Kernberg, try to change drive theory so that relational matters are accommodated, but in a way that is ultimately instinctual. Or, like Sullivan and Fairbairn, one can dispense with drive theory altogether and begin anew with interpersonal relations as the cornerstone.

Introduction

VANN SPRUIELL, IN HIS REVIEW of Freud's concept of idealization, mentions that "Freud never concentrated on idealization as a subject. Instead, he took it up in passing as part of his concern with larger matters" (1979, p. 778). When Freud did speak explicitly of idealization, it was usually in the context of his ideas about narcissism. In addition, implicit meanings of idealization can be gleaned in the development of Freud's concepts of internalization and structure building.

As happened with so much of Freud's thought, those who followed him were wont to take up one idea or another and elaborate it along the lines of their own interests and proclivities, so that we have several Freudian systems, varying in emphasis and sometimes verging on incompatibility. With regards to idealization, psychoanalysts working in the United States who were roughly grouped together under the rubric of ego psychology, addressed themselves mainly to the developmental and structure-building potential of idealization. Theirs was, in a sense, a benign construction. Narcissism, seen by Freud as an original given of human equipment, was seen by them as a perhaps ambiguous immaturity which needed to be both attenuated and made use of in the course of growth. Idealization, as an expression of narcissism, could optimally be transformed into an investment in ideals which could act as influence and spur for internal development. IN ADDITION TO ANY GENERAL INTEREST inherent in an account of subjective experience, I hope that this paper may be of value in appraising the relative effectiveness of psychoanalytic therapy in dealing with obstinate human emotional disturbances. In addition to my reflections on the analysis itself, I quote from a number of letters which Guntrip wrote to me afterwards—certainly an aid to what he often called "postanalytic improvement."

When I first saw Harry Guntrip in 1964, he was still, at the age of 62, dealing with his own psychological problems, despite his having gained by then an international reputation, both as therapist and as a writer and theoretician. This reputation was later to grow with the inclusion of another major book (Guntrip, 1968), as well as a slighter volume (Guntrip, 1971), and flowered with invitations to lecture at major psychoanalytic centres in Britain and in the United States. At that time, after just over 1,000 hours of analysis with Fairbairn, Guntrip was still troubled by periodic exhaustion-illnesses which were quite debilitating. These illnesses were invariably triggered off by the death or departure of a close friend and seemed to be connected with the severe trauma, at the age of three and one half, over the death of Guntrip's younger brother, for which he had had total amnesia. THE TENDENCY TO VIEW THE mother-infant relationship as being ideal is virtually universal, transcending the boundaries of culture and geography. Not only does this image dominate in primitive societies, but it is also the centerpiece of Christianity, where icons of the Virgin Mother swaddling the infant Christ are familiar. And yet, buried in that image of perfect harmony and bliss, other forces of a dark and destructive nature may be present as well. These sinister forces of maternal rage are encountered in cases of infant physical and sexual abuse, announced in lurid tabloid headlines describing mothers who have suffocated or strangled their infants, evidently while in the throes of depressive or psychotic episodes.

For most of us, these images are repellent and it is relatively easy to condemn the perpetrators of these crimes who have vented forces of seemingly irrational anger against innocent babies. We are incredulous at their ability to harm that which is so precious and unable to defend itself and can only attribute these behaviors to the most disturbed psychological conditions. WHY DOES ANALYSIS TAKE SO LONG? Why do patients not get well as soon as we convey our dynamic understanding to them? Why does "insight" not necessarily lead to change, and what is it that the analyst or the patient must do to bring about desired change? These are the questions which Freud was trying to answer in writing of working through. Freud considered the working through process to be the therapeutic factor effecting the greatest changes in the patient, and he believed that it was working through which distinguished psychoanalysis from treatment by suggestion. Nevertheless, Freud was vague in defining what was meant by the term "working through," and while it has been considered an essential element of psychoanalytic technique, it has remained a misunderstood and confusing term. As psychoanalysis has evolved from a quasi-biological drive theory, through the development of ego-psychology, to the state of theoretical pluralism which characterizes contemporary psychoanalysis, the use of the term working through has been modified reflecting these theoretical revisions.

I propose the term "working toward" to capture the sense of the work of both patient and analyst as "coparticipants" (Wolstein, 1983) in the analytic process. Patient and analyst not only work toward a new and "corrective" relationship, but work toward making the nuances of that relationship explicit.

In a follow-up to this paper the author will examine the implications of Piaget's account of the gradual accommodation of schemata, and particularly of the development of logical operations, for a clinical understanding of the nature of change in the psychoanalytic process.

Peter Shabad  

Introduction

THE UNDERLYING THEME OF THIS paper is that struggles for proprietorship of the terrain of reality are not so much a matter of intellectual discourse, but instead reflect different means of coping with wish and disillusionment.

For some time I have been struck by the fervor with which many patients use the pretense of "being realistic" in order to shield precious, often "unrealistic" wishes from disillusionment. It seems often that an enormous psychic effort is required before these patients can express their wishes overtly without disclaimers such as, "But that will never happen, " or "That's not realistic." When the patient is finally able to voice a deeply held wish, and in the next breath adds, "Okay, so what do I do now?" we see how the previously defensive preoccupation with reality concerns quickly gives way to a call to some action toward the fulfillment of the wish. For the patient, the use of pragmatism had been defensively superimposed upon the wishes tucked away in the unconscious. These unconscious wishes, unmodified by the processes of genuine disillusionment and mourning, remain inextricably intertwined with their fulfillment in external reality. Freud (1911) noted that "unconscious processes equate reality of thought with external actuality, and wishes with their fulfillment" (p. 225).

An earlier version of this paper was presented at the Spring Meeting of the Division of Psychoanalysis of the American Psychological Association, Boston, April, 1989.

In this presentation we have an example of analytic work in trouble, and the term employed to describe this trouble reveals underlying assumptions about how we understand the analytic process when it is going well.

Webster's gives two definitions for "stalemate"; one is: "… any situation making further action impossible …" The analytic process is a form of action, and things should be moving, going somewhere, we tend to feel. When things are stalemated, stuck, deadlocked, there is something wrong. The other definition of "stalemate" is: "in chess, the position of the king when so situated that, though not in check, he cannot move without being placed in check, there being no other available move; it results in a draw." (p. 1770) The analytic process is like a chessgame, a mock war. Freud introduced this metaphor in 1913, and it has served us well ever since. What is the analyst's king, that extremely vulnerable but indispensable piece without which there is no game? I think we would have to say the analyst's king is "understanding", and that this case is one in which the analyst's understanding is being attacked from all sides.

The patient's experience from the very beginning is filled with self-hatred and self-attack, reflecting two ways of organizing her internal experience or, as Sullivan would put it, two "personifications" of self. One version of herself, narcissistic, intellectual and sadistic, apparently organized around an identification with her father's intellectuality and contemptuous criticism, is continually attacking another version of herself, ineffectual, passive and incompetent, apparently organized around an identification with her mother's actual incompetence (as well as the latter's role as foil for the father).

Amnon Issacharoff M.D.

Amnon Issacharoff

Amnon Issacharoff  

Introduction

PSYCHOANALYSIS STARTED AS a therapeutic modality by curing symptoms. When psychoanalysts widened their scope, inevitably the patient and his way of being in the world, became more and more the treatment issue. Today every analysis becomes character analysis sooner or later. The patient's and the analyst's personalities are exposed to and bruised by each other. In this process, they are either bogged down by transference and counter-transference issues, that is, character-determined issues, or emerge somewhat re-shaped by the encounter. No patient's character reframing takes place without a corresponding accommodation on the analyst's part. Each one, patient and analyst, has a different purpose and way of approaching the situation, but both participants have to change. This intent is acknowledged by the patient and intrinsic to his role. As I see interpersonal psychoanalysis, the psychoanalyst recognizes the inevitability of the immersion of his own character issues in the therapeutic process and responds in his own unique way to the challenges of every dyad. In this kind of chess game both players play instinctively the opening gambits. Character traits and temperament frame and color the patient's initial presentation and the analyst's initial technical moves. After the infinite variations of the middle game, a successful outcome is not unsimilar to a chess match. One player hopefully "loses" after his defenses are penetrated. For the loser giving up the king is necessary for a new and better beginning. The other player "wins, " but only after a protracted struggle and making sacrifices.
